issues.claim: Chunk title: 'Hardship changes confirmed in writing and enforcement paused'
issues.evidence: INFO 105 (updated May 2025) covers written notice of changes ('no later than 30 days after the date of the agreement') but does not address pausing enforcement after a hardship notice; the body also says nothing about enforcement.

issues.claim: For credit complaints involving default notices, hardship notices or requests to postpone enforcement, the maximum is 21 calendar days.
issues.evidence: RG 271 Table 1 (hardship notices / postponement): 'No later than 21 calendar days after receiving the complaint. Exceptions apply if the credit provider or lessor does not have sufficient information to make a decision, or if they reach an agreement with the complainant.' With insufficient information the provider can request it within 21 days and then has 'a further 21 calendar days' (or 7 days if not received within 21 days), so 21 days is not an absolute maximum for hardship complaints. Missing condition changes meaning.
issues.suggested_fix: For credit complaints involving default notices, the maximum is 21 calendar days. For complaints involving hardship notices or requests to postpone enforcement proceedings, it is also 21 calendar days, but exceptions apply if the credit provider does not have sufficient information to make a decision (it must request the information within 21 calendar days, then has a further 21 calendar days after receiving it, or 7 calendar days if it is not provided within 21 calendar days) or if it reaches an agreement with the complainant (30 calendar days to confirm the terms in writing).

issues.claim: Within 10 business days, if the funds are available, the receiving bank must return them within 5 business days if practicable and no later than 10 business days, without needing the recipient's consent.
issues.evidence: ePayments Code cl 30.1-30.3: the process applies where the user reports within 10 business days 'and the sending ADI is satisfied that: (a) a mistaken internet payment has occurred, and (b) there are sufficient funds available'; cl 30.2 'If satisfied that a mistaken internet payment has occurred, the receiving ADI must return the funds ... within 5 business days ... if practicable, or such longer period as is reasonably necessary, up to a maximum of 10 business days.' cl 30.3: if not satisfied, it 'may seek the consent of the unintended recipient'. The chunk drops the 'satisfied a mistaken internet payment has occurred' condition, implying return is automatic.
issues.suggested_fix: Within 10 business days, if both banks are satisfied a mistaken internet payment has occurred and sufficient funds are available in the recipient's account, the receiving bank must return the funds within 5 business days if practicable, or up to a maximum of 10 business days, without needing the recipient's consent. If the receiving bank is not satisfied, it may seek the recipient's consent to return the funds.

issues.claim: ...or more often if you have recently been rejected for credit.
issues.evidence: Live Moneysmart page says only: 'you have a right to get a copy of your credit report for free every 3 months.' The phrases 'more often'/'more frequently' do not appear; the only use of 'rejected' is 'understand why a lender rejected you'. (The research-note quote 'or more frequently if you provide evidence that you have been rejected for credit recently' is not on this page.)
issues.suggested_fix: Moneysmart says you have a right to get a copy of your credit report for free every 3 months.

issues.claim: Moneysmart says anyone who has been scammed should ... contact IDCARE on 1800 595 160 for a free response plan.
issues.evidence: IDCARE appears only under the heading 'What should you do if a scammer has your personal information?' ('If you think the scammer has your personal details (like name, phone, email, address, identity documents), here's what to do'), with 'Call 1800 595 160 (Monday to Friday, 8am-5pm)' and 'They can help you make a plan (for free) to limit the damage.' It is not a step for everyone scammed.
issues.suggested_fix: Moneysmart says anyone who has been scammed should contact their bank or card provider immediately to report the scam, report the scam to Scamwatch to help protect others, and change passwords. If a scammer has your personal details, IDCARE (1800 595 160, Monday to Friday, 8am-5pm) can help you make a plan, for free, to limit the damage.
